1.q: Kai buys 3 rulers at $4 each and a story book for $9. He pays with $50. How much change does he get?
1.hint: Find the cost of the 3 rulers first.
1.why: 3 rulers cost 3 × $4 = $12. With the book that is $12 + $9 = $21. Change: $50 − $21 = $29.

1.q: A story book has 30 pages. The page numbers start at 1 and go up to 30. How many digits are printed in the page numbers altogether?
1.hint: Pages 1 to 9 have one digit each. Pages 10 and up have two digits each.
1.why: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits. Pages 10 to 30 are 21 pages with 2 digits each, which is 42 digits. 9 + 42 = 51 digits.

1.q: A string of flags has this colour pattern again and again: red, white, white, red, white, white, ... What colour is the 20th flag?
1.hint: Each pattern has 3 flags. Write the pattern out in rows of 3.
1.why: The pattern repeats after every 3 flags. 18 is a multiple of 3, so the 18th flag ends a pattern. The 20th flag is the 2nd flag of a new pattern, which is white.

1.q: Kai practises the piano for 1 hour and 35 minutes. How many minutes did he practise in all?
1.hint: One hour is 60 minutes. Change the hour to minutes first.
1.why: 1 hour is 60 minutes. 60 + 35 = 95 minutes.

1.q: Mei takes one token from bag A and one from bag B. Each bag has tokens numbered 1 to 7. The two numbers add up to 10. Count A3 with B7 and A7 with B3 as different. How many different ways can this happen?
1.hint: List the numbers from bag A in order, starting with the smallest one that can work. For each one, ask what the number from bag B must be.
1.why: The pairs (bag A, bag B) are 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5, 6 and 4, and 7 and 3. That is 5 ways.

1.q: Lamp posts along a path are marked with how many metres they are from the gate. One lamp post is at 16 m and another is at 56 m. A bench is exactly halfway between them. How many metres from the gate is the bench?
1.hint: Find how far apart the two lamp posts are. Half of that is how far the bench is from each post.
1.why: The posts are 56 − 16 = 40 m apart. Half of 40 is 20. The bench is 20 m from the first post, so it is 16 + 20 = 36 m from the gate.

1.q: Ben has 92 marbles and Siti has 45 marbles. How many more marbles does Ben have than Siti?
1.hint: Take the smaller number away from the bigger number.
1.why: 92 − 45 = 47 marbles. Ben has 47 marbles more than Siti.

1.q: Two trays hold the same number of counters. The first tray has 28 red counters and 15 blue counters. The second tray has 16 yellow counters and some green counters. How many green counters are there?
1.hint: Find how many counters are in the first tray. The second tray must have the same.
1.why: 28 + 15 = 43. The second tray must also have 43, so 16 + 27 = 43. So 27 counters are green.

1.q: A number chart shows 1 to 100 in order, with 10 numbers in each row. Zack puts a counter on 34. He moves it down 3 rows, then right 2 squares, then up 1 row. Which number is the counter on now?
1.hint: Moving down one row adds 10. Moving right one square adds 1.
1.why: 34 + 30 = 64 after going down 3 rows. Then 64 + 2 = 66. Going up 1 row takes away 10: 66 − 10 = 56.

1.q: A model boat costs $9 at both Shop A and Shop B. Shop B gives 1 boat free for every 3 boats you buy. Dina needs 8 boats and shops where she pays less. How much does she pay?
1.hint: Work out what Dina pays at Shop A. Then work out what she pays at Shop B.
1.why: Shop A: 8 × $9 = $72. At Shop B every 4 boats cost only 3 boats' money, so 8 boats cost 2 × 3 × $9 = $54. Shop B is cheaper, so Dina pays $54.

1.q: A parcel has the number 61 on its label. A helper reads the two digits in the wrong order. How far apart are the number on the label and the number the helper reads?
1.hint: Write the number with its two digits the other way round. Then take the smaller number away from the bigger one.
1.why: Read the wrong way round, 61 becomes 16. 61 − 16 = 45.

1.q: Mei makes a paper chain by sticking 6 strips in a line. Each strip is 5 cm long. Where two strips meet, 1 cm of one strip lies on top of the other. How long is the finished chain?
1.hint: Add up the lengths of all the strips. Then take away the part that is hidden at each join.
1.why: 6 strips are 6 × 5 = 30 cm. There are 5 joins and each hides 1 cm, so 5 cm is hidden. 30 − 5 = 25 cm.

1.q: Aisha cuts a round biscuit in two equal pieces with one straight cut through the middle. What shape is each piece: a circle, a half circle, a quarter circle or a triangle?
1.hint: Look at the cut edge. Is it straight or curved? Then look at the rest of the edge.
1.why: The cut edge is 1 straight side, and the rest of the edge is 1 curved edge. A circle has no straight side and a triangle has no curved edge. Each piece is a half circle.

1.q: Fill a 3 by 3 grid with 1, 2 and 3. Every row and every column must have each number once. The top-left square is 1 and the middle square is 3. What number goes in the bottom-left square?
1.hint: Fill the top row first. Which number cannot go above the 3?
1.why: Top row: 1, 2, 3. Middle row: 2, 3, 1. Bottom row: 3, 1, 2. The bottom-left square holds 3.

1.q: Siti writes the numbers one, two, three and so on up to ten in words. How many letters does she write in all?
1.hint: Count the letters in each word and add them up. The word "one" has 3 letters.
1.why: one 3, two 3, three 5, four 4, five 4, six 3, seven 5, eight 5, nine 4, ten 3. Adding: 3 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 39 letters.

1.q: Four of these numbers are in one times table. One number is not: 15, 25, 35, 45 and 52. Which one is it?
1.hint: Try the times tables one at a time. Which one has four of the five numbers?
1.why: 15, 25, 35 and 45 are all in the 5 times table, but 52 is not. The number that does not belong is 52.

1.q: A strip of card lies along a ruler. One end of the strip is at the 2 cm mark. The other end is at the 30 cm mark. How long is the strip?
1.hint: Careful: the strip does not start at zero. Work out the difference between the two marks.
1.why: The strip is 30 − 2 = 28 cm long.

1.q: A running track has 20 cones, numbered 1 to 20 in order, going round the track. Which cone is exactly opposite cone number 9?
1.hint: Opposite means halfway round the track. How many cones are in half of the circle?
1.why: Half of 20 is 10. Count on 10 places from 9: 9 + 10 = 19.

1.q: Mei and Ben collect stickers on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Mei got 12 on Friday. Ben got 11 on Sunday. Together they got 20 on Friday, 57 on Saturday and 25 on Sunday. Mei got 35 in all. How many stickers did Ben get on Saturday?
1.hint: Draw a table with two rows and three columns. Fill in the numbers you know. Then find what you can.
1.why: Mei got 25 − 11 = 14 on Sunday, because the two children got 25 together. Then Mei got 35 − 12 − 14 = 9 on Saturday. On Saturday they got 57 together, so Ben got 57 − 9 = 48 stickers.

1.q: A sticker covers one digit in this sum: 4? + 25 = 71. Which digit is under the sticker?
1.hint: Look at the ones column: 5 plus what digit gives a number that ends in 1?
1.why: In the ones column, 5 plus the hidden digit must end in 1. 5 + 6 = 11 does, so the digit is 6. Check: 46 + 25 = 71.

1.q: Mei empties her money box. It holds 3 twenty-cent coins and 2 ten-cent coins. What is the total in cents?
1.hint: Find the cents in the twenty-cent coins first. Then add the cents in the ten-cent coins.

1.q: Aunty sells eggs in trays of 10. She has 4 full trays and 17 extra eggs in a bag. How many eggs is that altogether?
1.hint: Each full tray holds 10 eggs. Count the eggs on the trays first.
1.why: 4 trays of 10 is 4 × 10 = 40 eggs. Add the extra eggs: 40 + 17 = 57 eggs.

1.q: A star and a moon each stand for a whole number. Star + star = 18. Star + moon = 44. What number does the moon stand for?
1.hint: Find the star first. Then use it in the second line.

1.q: Zack leaves school and walks 6 blocks north, then 5 blocks east, then 3 blocks south. The roads run in straight lines along the blocks. What is the fewest number of blocks he must walk along the roads to get back to school?
1.hint: Work out how far north or south of the school Zack is now, and how far east or west.
1.why: Zack walked 6 blocks north and then 3 blocks south, so he is 6 − 3 = 3 blocks north of school. He is 5 blocks east. To get back he must go 3 blocks south and 5 blocks west: 3 + 5 = 8 blocks.

1.q: Ali, Siti and Ravi each bring one fruit to school: a mango, a papaya or a banana. Ali brings neither the mango nor the papaya. Siti does not bring the mango. Who brings the mango?
1.hint: Start with the friend who has only one fruit left to choose from.
1.why: Ali brings neither the mango nor the papaya, so Ali brings the banana. Siti does not bring the mango and the banana is taken, so Siti brings the papaya. Ravi brings the mango. So Ravi brings the mango.

1.q: A drummer plays a song with 35 beats. She hits the cymbal on every beat in the 5 times table. That is beat 5, beat 10, beat 15 and so on. How many times does she hit the cymbal?
1.hint: Count on in fives: 5, 10, 15 and so on, until you pass 35.
1.why: The cymbal beats are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35. That is 7 hits.

1.q: Zack sorts these numbers: 17, 24, 8, 39, 42, 31, 26, 55, 12 and 48. He keeps only the numbers that are odd and bigger than 20. How many numbers does he keep?
1.hint: Check each number twice: is it odd, and is it bigger than 20?
1.why: The numbers that pass both checks are 39, 31, 55. That is 3 numbers.

1.q: Aisha faces west. She turns right, then right again, then right again. Which way does she face now: north, east, south or west?
1.hint: Draw a small compass. Turn one step at a time and write the direction after each turn.
1.why: Facing west, then north, then east, then south. After the three turns Aisha faces south.

1.q: A toy robot starts on square 21 of a number track. It moves forward 15, then back 8, then forward 25. Which square is the robot on now?
1.hint: Move one step at a time on the number track, or add and take away.
1.why: The squares in order are 21, 36, 28, 53. The robot ends on square 53.

1.q: Priya is taller than Hui Min. Arjun is taller than Priya. Who is the shortest?
1.hint: Draw three lines. Make the shortest person's line the shortest.
1.why: Priya is taller than Hui Min, and Arjun is taller than Priya. From tallest: Arjun, Priya, Hui Min. So Hui Min is the shortest.

1.q: A library shelf has 5 rows of 6 books. Then 3 more books are put on the table beside it. How many books are there altogether?
1.hint: Find the books on the shelf first. Then add the books on the table.
1.why: 5 rows of 6 books make 30 books. Add the 3 more books: 33 books.

2.q: A scarf has stripes in this pattern again and again: gold, green, green, gold, blue. The scarf has 47 stripes. How many of the stripes are green?
2.hint: Each pattern has 5 stripes. Count the green stripes in one pattern, then count the full patterns.
2.why: There are 9 full patterns with 2 green stripes each: 9 × 2 = 18. The last 2 stripes are gold and green, which adds 1 green stripe. 18 + 1 = 19 stripes.

2.q: Ana, Ben, Cai and Dev play games 1 to 4 in four rounds. In every round the four friends play four different games, and each friend plays every game once. The timetable shows what we know, and ? means we do not know yet. Which game does Ana play in round 4?
2.hint: In round 1, Cai and Dev play games 3 and 4, in some order. Use the other clues to decide which is which.
2.why: The full timetable, in the order Ana, Ben, Cai, Dev, is: round 1: 1, 2, 4, 3. Round 2: 2, 3, 1, 4. Round 3: 3, 4, 2, 1. Round 4: 4, 1, 3, 2. Ana plays game 4 in round 4.
2.code:
Ana Ben Cai Dev
Round 1:   1   2   ?   ?
Round 2:   ?   ?   1   ?
Round 3:   3   ?   ?   ?
Round 4:   ?   ?   ?   2

2.q: A school store keeps pencils in boxes of 100, packs of 10 and single pencils. It has 4 boxes, 3 packs and 7 single pencils. How many pencils is that altogether?
2.hint: Work out how many pencils are in the boxes, then in the packs. Then add the single pencils.
2.why: 4 boxes make 400 pencils and 3 packs make 30 pencils. 400 + 30 + 7 = 437 pencils.

2.q: Mum buys 3 kg 40 g of flour for baking. How many grams of flour is that?
2.hint: One kilogram is 1000 grams. Change the kilograms to grams first.

2.q: A lily patch covers 3 square metres of a pond in week 1. The patch doubles in size every week. How many square metres does it cover in week 5?
2.hint: Doubling means two times as big. Write down the size for each week.
2.why: Week 1 is 3, then doubling each week: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. Week 5 is 48 m².

2.q: A chocolate bar has 4 rows of 7 squares. Each snap breaks one piece into two pieces along a line. How many snaps are needed to break the bar into single squares?
2.hint: Each snap makes one more piece. How many pieces do you want at the end?
2.why: At the start there is 1 piece. At the end there are 28 pieces. Each snap makes one more piece, so 28 − 1 = 27 snaps are needed.

2.q: 2A and 2B recycled paper for three weeks. 2A recycled 18 kg in week 1. 2B recycled 27 kg in week 3. 2A recycled 58 kg and 2B recycled 72 kg in all. Weeks 1, 2 and 3 gave 30, 50 and 50 kg in all. How many kg did 2B recycle in week 2?
2.hint: Draw a table with two rows and three columns. Fill in what you know. Then find the missing numbers one at a time.
2.why: Week 1: 2B recycled 30 − 18 = 12 kg. Then in week 2, 2B recycled 72 − 12 − 27 = 33 kg.

2.q: A florist ties 5 ribbons together in one long line. Each ribbon is 10 cm long. At every knot, 2 cm of ribbon is used up in the knot. How long is the line of ribbons?
2.hint: Add the lengths of all the ribbons first. Then think about how many knots there are.
2.why: 5 ribbons are 5 × 10 = 50 cm. There are 4 knots and each uses 2 cm, so 8 cm is used up. 50 − 8 = 42 cm.

2.q: Dina picks up a solid shape from the toy box. It has no flat face at all. Is it a cube, a cone, a cylinder or a sphere?
2.hint: Think about the flat faces of each solid. Which solid has none?
2.why: A cube has 6 flat faces, a cone has 1 and a cylinder has 2. A solid with no flat face at all is a sphere.

2.q: A cooking class starts at 7:55 and lasts 50 minutes. At which hour does the class end? Give the hour only, like 9 for 9:20.
2.hint: Add the minutes first. How many minutes past 7:55 is the end of the class? Remember that 60 minutes make 1 hour.
2.why: 7:55 and 5 more minutes is 8:00. There are 45 minutes left to add, so the class ends at 8:45. The hour is 8.

2.q: A balance scale is level. The left pan holds weights of 63 g and 29 g. The right pan holds a 45 g weight and one more weight. How heavy is the extra weight?
2.hint: Add up the left pan first. The right pan must weigh the same.
2.why: 63 + 29 = 92. The right pan must also weigh 92 g, so 45 + 47 = 92. The extra weight is 47 g.

2.q: Bridges join four islands. The bridge lengths in kilometres are: Pier to Hill 12. Pier to Cove 8. Cove to Hill 3. Hill to Dock 9. Cove to Dock 16. What is the shortest way from Pier to Dock, in kilometres?
2.hint: List the different routes from Pier to Dock. Add the bridge lengths for each route.
2.why: The routes are Pier-Hill-Dock 21, Pier-Cove-Dock 24, and Pier-Cove-Hill-Dock 8 + 3 + 9 = 20. The shortest is 20 km.

2.q: Kai is faster than Zack. Mira is faster than Kai. Zack is faster than Lena. Who came second in the race?
2.hint: Put the four names in a row from the fastest runner to the slowest runner.
2.why: From fastest to slowest: Mira, Kai, Zack, Lena. Kai came second.

2.q: A shop stacks tins in rows. The top row has 3 tins, and each lower row has 1 more tin than the row above it. The bottom row has 10 tins. How many tins are in the stack?
2.hint: Pair the top row with the bottom row, the second row with the one above the bottom, and so on.
2.why: The rows have 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 tins. Pairs: 3 + 10, 4 + 9, 5 + 8, 6 + 7. Each pair is 13. 4 pairs make 52 tins.

2.q: A bag of rice weighs 5 kg 200 g. Aunty uses 1 kg 750 g of the rice for a party. How many grams of rice are left in the bag?
2.hint: Change each mass to grams first. One kilogram is 1000 grams.

2.q: Two class libraries have 84 books together. Library A has 18 more books than Library B. How many books does Library A have?
2.hint: If the two libraries had the same number of books, each would have half. Then move some books across.
2.why: Library A has 51 books and Library B has 33. They add to 84 and differ by 18. So Library A has 51 books.

2.q: Two whole numbers add up to 13. When you multiply them, the answer is 40. What is the bigger of the two numbers?
2.hint: List pairs that add up to 13, such as 6 and 7, then 4 and 9. Multiply each pair until you reach 40.
2.why: 5 and 8 add up to 13 and multiply to 40. The bigger number is 8.

2.q: Two players take turns to take 1, 2 or 3 sticks from a pile of 26 sticks. The player who takes the last stick wins. You go first. How many sticks should you take now to be sure of winning?
2.hint: Try to leave a multiple of 4 sticks for your friend. Then copy your friend's move to make 4 each round.
2.why: Take away 2 sticks to leave 24, which is a multiple of 4. Whatever your friend takes, you take enough to make 4 in that round, and you take the last stick.

2.q: A cupboard has 7 drawers with 9 pencils in each drawer. Then 5 pencils are taken out. How many pencils are left in the cupboard?
2.hint: Find the number of pencils in all the drawers first. Then take away the pencils taken out.
2.why: 7 drawers of 9 pencils make 63 pencils. Take away 5: 63 − 5 = 58 pencils.

2.q: At a cafe, Priya buys 3 cups of barley water at $3 each and a slice of cake for $4. She pays with $20. How much change does she get?
2.hint: Find the cost of the 3 cups first.
2.why: 3 cups cost 3 × $3 = $9. With the cake: $9 + $4 = $13. Change: $20 − $13 = $7.

2.q: How many edges do two cubes and four cuboids have altogether?
2.hint: Count the edges of one solid at a time. Then add.
2.why: A cube has 12 edges and a cuboid has 12 edges too, so each of the 6 solids has 12 edges. 6 × 12 = 72 edges.

2.q: A long strip of paper is folded in half four times in a row. Then one straight cut is made across the middle of the folded strip. When the strip is opened up, how many separate pieces are there?
2.hint: After 1 fold the strip has 2 layers. Think about how the layers grow, and how many cut marks the open strip shows.
2.why: 4 folds make 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 layers, so the cut goes through 16 places on the open strip. 16 cuts make 16 + 1 = 17 pieces.

2.q: Farhan counts in 4s, starting at 4: 4, 8, 12 and so on. He stops when he says 72. How many numbers does he say?
2.hint: Count in 4s: 4, 8, 12 and so on. You can also ask how many 4s fit into 72.
2.why: The numbers are 4, 8, 12, ... up to 72. 72 = 18 × 4, so Farhan says 18 numbers.

2.q: Dina, Arjun, Hui Min and Wei each order a different drink: barley, soya, juice or water. Dina orders neither the barley, the soya nor the water. Arjun orders neither the barley nor the water. Hui Min does not order the water. Who orders the water?
2.hint: Dina has only one drink left to choose from. Then see who else is left.
2.why: Dina orders the juice, Arjun orders the soya, Hui Min orders the barley, Wei orders the water. So Wei orders the water.

2.q: A water tank holds 42 litres at the start of Monday. On the next four days, it gets 13, then loses 35, then gets 27, then loses 39. What is the most water the tank holds at any time?
2.hint: Write down the amount in the tank after each day. Then pick the biggest.
2.why: The amounts in order are 42, 55, 20, 47, 8. The most is 55 litres.

2.q: A garden is a rectangle 20 m long and 11 m wide. Uncle puts a fence all the way round the edge of the garden. How long is the fence?
2.hint: The fence goes along all four sides. Add the two lengths and the two widths.
2.why: Two lengths: 2 × 20 = 40. Two widths: 2 × 11 = 22. The fence is 40 + 22 = 62 m.

2.q: Siti has 230 beads. Ahmad has 85 fewer beads than Siti. Kim has 120 more beads than Ahmad. How many beads does Kim have?
2.hint: Find Ahmad's beads first.
2.why: Ahmad has 230 − 85 = 145. Kim has 145 + 120 = 265 beads.

2.q: Aina, Ben and Chen each have a cake of the same size. Aina eats 1/4 of a cake, Ben eats 1/8 of a cake and Chen eats 1/3 of a cake. Who eats the smallest piece?
2.hint: The more equal pieces a cake is cut into, the smaller each piece is.
2.why: A cake cut into 8 equal pieces has smaller pieces than a cake cut into 4 or into 3. So 1/8 is the smallest piece, and Ben eats it.

2.q: Notebooks cost $6 each. A pack of 5 notebooks costs $25. A school needs 15 notebooks. How many dollars does it save by buying packs instead of single notebooks?
2.hint: Work out the cost with single notebooks. Then work out how many packs are needed.
2.why: Single: 15 × $6 = $90. Packs: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 packs, 3 × $25 = $75. The school saves $90 − $75 = $15.

2.q: Mei Ling sorts these numbers: 19, 27, 33, 48, 18, 52, 36, 21, 63 and 42. She keeps only the numbers that are in the 3 times table and bigger than 25. How many numbers does she keep?
2.hint: Check each number twice: is it in the 3 times table, and is it bigger than 25?
2.why: The numbers that pass both checks are 27, 33, 48, 36, 63, 42. That is 6 numbers.

2.q: A beetle crawls on a floor made of square tiles. It starts at a corner mark, crawls 9 tiles east, then 4 tiles north, then 3 tiles west. The tile lines are the only paths it may use. What is the fewest number of tiles it must crawl to get back to the corner mark?
2.hint: Work out how far east or west of the mark the beetle is now, and how far north or south.
2.why: East 9 and west 3 leave the beetle 9 − 3 = 6 tiles east of the mark. It is also 4 tiles north. To get back it must crawl 6 tiles west and 4 tiles south: 6 + 4 = 10 tiles.

3.q: Class 3A collected 250 cans. Class 3B collected 130 more cans than Class 3A. Class 3C collected 45 fewer cans than Class 3B. How many cans did the three classes collect altogether?
3.hint: Find the cans for Class 3B first. Then Class 3C. Then add all three.

3.q: A school sold raffle tickets on four days. It sold 126 on Friday, 238 on Saturday, 184 on Sunday and 97 on Monday. How many tickets were sold altogether?
3.hint: Add two days at a time. Add the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones.

3.q: A jar has 1000 buttons. 350 of them are red and 275 of them are blue. The rest are yellow. How many yellow buttons are in the jar?
3.hint: Add the red and blue buttons first. Then find how many more make 1000.

3.q: A raffle uses ticket numbers from 100 to 199. A ticket wins a prize if its three digits add up to 8. How many tickets win a prize?
3.hint: Every ticket starts with 1. What must the other two digits add up to?
3.why: The other two digits must add up to 8 − 1 = 7. The pairs are 0 and 7, 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, and then 4 and 3, 5 and 2, 6 and 1, 7 and 0. The winning tickets are 107, 116, 125, 134, 143, 152, 161 and 170, which is 8 tickets.

3.q: 10 children are at a puzzle club. Each pair of children shakes hands exactly once. How many handshakes happen?
3.hint: Each child shakes hands with 10 − 1 others, but each handshake has two children in it.
3.why: Each of the 10 children shakes 9 hands, which makes 90. Each handshake was counted twice, so 90 ÷ 2 = 45 handshakes.

3.q: In the number 6,482, how much more is the value of the digit 6 than the value of the digit 4?
3.hint: The 6 is in the thousands place and the 4 is in the hundreds place. Write the value of each.

3.q: 5 friends sit in a row of 5 chairs, one friend on each chair. In how many different ways can they be seated?
3.hint: Choose who sits on the first chair. Then see how many friends are left for the second chair.
3.why: 5 choices for the first chair, then 4, then 3, then 2, then 1. 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 ways.

3.q: Ali, Ben, Chen and Dina each play one instrument in the school band: piano, violin, guitar or drums. Ali does not play piano or drums. Ben plays violin. Chen does not play piano. Dina does not play guitar. Who plays piano?
3.hint: Ben plays violin, so nobody else does. Then work out who can play each remaining instrument.
3.why: Ali plays guitar, Ben plays violin, Chen plays drums, Dina plays piano. So Dina plays piano.

3.q: Hui Min has four digit cards: 2, 5, 7 and 9. She arranges all four into two 2-digit numbers and adds them. What greatest total can she make?
3.hint: The biggest digits should go in the tens places.
3.why: Put 9 and 7 in the tens places and 5 and 2 in the ones places: 72 + 95 = 167.

3.q: Mia's moneybox holds $12. On day 1 she puts in $8. On day 2 she takes out $3. She goes on putting in and taking out in turns, one change each day. How many dollars are in the moneybox at the end of day 23?
3.hint: Look at two days together. What is the change in the moneybox after one putting in and one taking out?
3.why: Two days (putting in $8, taking out $3) change the moneybox by 8 − 3 = $5. 23 days are 11 pairs of days and 1 more day. The 11 pairs add 11 × 5 = $55, and the extra day adds $8. So the moneybox holds $12 + $55 + $8 = $75.

3.q: A square poster has an area of 144 square centimetres. Hui Min wants to glue a ribbon along its edge, once round. What length of ribbon does she need?
3.hint: A square has 4 equal sides. Which number multiplied by itself makes 144?
3.why: 12 × 12 = 144, so each side is 12 cm. The ribbon goes round 4 sides: 4 × 12 = 48 cm.

3.q: A hot-air balloon is 20 m above the ground. It goes up by 5, then down by 12, then up by 9, then down by 3. What is the greatest height above the ground that the balloon reaches, in metres?
3.hint: Write down the height after each change. Then find the biggest.
3.why: The heights in order are 20, 25, 13, 22, 19. The greatest height is 25 m.

3.q: A vegetable plot is a rectangle 13 m long and 7 m wide. Each paving slab covers exactly 1 square metre. How many slabs are needed to cover the whole plot?
3.hint: Think of rows of slabs. How many rows? How many slabs in each row?
3.why: 7 rows with 13 slabs in each row: 7 × 13 = 91 slabs.

3.q: Dina has 25 beads to share between two necklaces. Each necklace needs at least 3 beads. The necklaces are not labelled, so 3 and 22 is the same as 22 and 3. In how many different ways can she share the beads?
3.hint: Start with the smallest number of beads that a necklace may have. Then try the next number, and keep going until the two necklaces would swap.

3.q: A market stall opens at 5 am and closes at 8 pm. For how many hours is the stall open each day?
3.hint: Count the hours from 5 am to 12 noon. Then count the hours from 12 noon to 8 pm.
3.why: From 5 am to 12 noon is 7 hours. From 12 noon to 8 pm is 8 hours. 7 + 8 = 15 hours.

3.q: A big fish weighs 2 kg 85 g. Write the mass of the fish in grams.
3.hint: One kilogram is 1000 grams. Change the kilograms to grams first.

3.q: In one month, the 5th is a Thursday. What is the date of the 3rd Tuesday in that month?
3.hint: Find the first Tuesday of the month. Then add 7 for each next one.
3.why: The first Tuesday is the 3rd. Adding 7 each time gives the 3rd, 10th and 17th. The 3rd Tuesday is the 17th.

3.q: Zack cycles 2 km 450 m in the morning and 1 km 800 m in the afternoon. How many metres does he cycle in the whole day?
3.hint: Change each distance to metres first. One kilometre is 1000 metres.

3.q: In a class of 53 children, 40 are in the swimming club and 38 are in the cycling club. 3 children are in neither club. How many children are in both clubs?
3.hint: Find how many children are in at least one club. Add the two clubs and compare.
3.why: 50 children are in at least one club. 40 + 38 = 78, and 78 is 28 more than 50. Those 28 were counted twice, so 28 children are in both.

3.q: A rectangular mat has an area of 364 square centimetres. It is 14 cm long. How wide is the mat?
3.hint: Area is length times width. Which number times 14 makes 364?
3.why: 14 × 26 cm = 364. The mat is 26 cm wide.

3.q: A cup of bubble tea costs $8 at Shop A. At Shop B, a cup costs $8 too, but you get 1 cup free for every 4 cups you buy. A club needs 20 cups. How many dollars does it save by using Shop B?
3.hint: Work out the cost at Shop A. At Shop B, find how many cups of every 5 you pay for.
3.why: Shop A: 20 × $8 = $160. At Shop B, 20 cups are 4 sets of 5 cups, and each set costs 4 × $8 = $32. So Shop B costs 4 × $32 = $128. The club saves $160 − $128 = $32.

3.q: A museum has two special exhibitions in March. The dinosaur show opens on 6 March and closes on 23 March. The space show opens on 10 March and closes on 30 March. Both shows are open on the day they open and the day they close. On how many days can a visitor see both shows?
3.hint: Find the first day when both shows are open, and the last day when both are open.
3.why: Both shows are open from the 10th to the 23rd. That is 23 − 10 + 1 = 14 days.

3.q: There are 301 people at a school fair. Each table seats 8 people. How many tables must be set up so that everyone has a seat?
3.hint: Divide the people by the seats at a table. What do you do with the remainder?
3.why: 37 tables seat 37 × 8 = 296 people. 5 people are left, and they need another table. So 38 tables must be set up.

3.q: Each letter stands for a different digit. AB + CB = BBC. AB and CB are 2-digit numbers and BBC is a 3-digit number. What digit is A?
3.hint: Two numbers with two digits each can never make 200 or more. What does that tell you about B?
3.why: B must be 1. In the ones place 1 + 1 = 2, so C = 2. In the tens place A + 2 must make 11, so A = 9. Check: 91 + 21 = 112.

3.q: Roads in kilometres: Home to Library 8. Home to Park 12. Library to Park 3. Library to Pool 13. Park to Pool 9. Park to School 17. Pool to School 7. Find the shortest way from Home to School, in kilometres.
3.hint: List the routes from Home to School and add up the road lengths on each one.
3.why: The best route is Home-Library-Park-Pool-School: 8 + 3 + 9 + 7 = 27 km. Home-Park-Pool-School is 12 + 9 + 7 = 28, which is longer.

3.q: A garden bed is divided into 3 equal strips and Ravi plants 2 of them with chillies. If the same bed had been divided into 12 equal strips, how many of those strips would hold the chillies?
3.hint: Cut each of the 3 big strips into smaller equal strips. How many small strips does each big strip make?
3.why: Each big strip makes 12 ÷ 3 = 4 small strips. 2 big strips are 2 × 4 = 8 strips.

3.q: Mei picks any six odd numbers and adds them all together. Will her total always be odd, or will it always be even?
3.hint: Try it with small numbers of your own, and add the numbers two at a time.
3.why: Two odd numbers add to an even number. Six numbers make three pairs, so the total is three even numbers added together, which is even.

3.q: Find the least 3-digit number in which the three digits add to 15.
3.hint: The hundreds digit should be as small as possible. Then make the tens digit small too.
3.why: Start with the hundreds digit 1. The other two digits must add to 14, so the tens digit should be as small as possible: 5 and 9. The number is 159.

3.q: A craft table sells bookmark kits. Each kit has one ribbon, one tassel and one charm. The table has 2 ribbons, 5 tassels and 4 charms. How many different bookmark kits can you make?
3.hint: Pick one ribbon. How many tassel and charm choices go with it?

3.q: Hana trains for a fun run for 9 weeks and 5 days. For how many days does she train in all?
3.hint: There are 7 days in a week. Change the weeks into days first.
3.why: A week has 7 days, so 9 weeks are 9 × 7 = 63 days. With 5 more days, Hana trains 63 + 5 = 68 days.

3.q: How many numbers from 50 to 200 are in the 8 times table?
3.hint: Find the first multiple of 8 that is more than 50. Then keep adding 8.
3.why: The multiples of 8 in this range are 56, 64, 72, ... 200. The first is 7 × 8 and the last is 25 × 8, so there are 25 − 7 + 1 = 19 numbers.

4.q: A hall clock gains 20 minutes in every real hour. At 9:00 am it is set exactly right. Later the clock shows that 240 minutes have passed since 9:00 am. How many minutes have really passed?
4.hint: In one real hour, the clock does not show 60 minutes. How many minutes does it show?
4.why: In 60 real minutes the clock shows 60 + 20 = 80 minutes. 240 ÷ 80 = 3, so 3 real hours have passed: 3 × 60 = 180 minutes.

4.q: A mural is painted on a rectangular wall that is 14 m long and 12 m high. What is the area of the wall, in square metres?
4.hint: The area of a rectangle is its length times its height.

4.q: A drone starts on the ground. It goes up 5 m, then down 1 m, then up 5 m, then down 1 m, and so on in turns. After how many moves is the drone first at a height of 57 m or more?
4.hint: Look at two moves together: up 5 m and down 1 m. The drone reaches each new highest point after an 'up' move.
4.why: Each pair of moves lifts the drone by 5 − 1 = 4 m. After 26 moves (13 pairs) it is at 52 m. The 27th move is an 'up' move: 52 + 5 = 57. So the drone first reaches 57 m after 27 moves.

4.q: A diver is 14 m below the surface of a lake. The diver goes deeper by 6, then back up by 9, then deeper by 15, then back up by 4. What is the greatest distance below the surface that the diver reaches? Answer in metres.
4.hint: Write the distance below the surface after each move. Then find the biggest.
4.why: The distances in order are 14, 20, 11, 26, 22. The greatest distance is 26 m.

4.q: Dina glues strips of card end to end to make a long banner. Every strip is 15 cm long, and each strip overlaps the next one by 3 cm. The finished banner is 243 cm long. How many strips does Dina use?
4.hint: The first strip gives its whole length. Every other strip adds the length that is not covered by the overlap.
4.why: Each new strip adds 15 − 3 = 12 cm. The first strip is 15 cm, so the other strips make 243 − 15 = 228 cm. 228 ÷ 12 = 19 more strips. 1 + 19 = 20 strips.

4.q: A school concert has 3 acts. Each act lasts 35 minutes. A break of 10 minutes comes between one act and the next, but not after the last act. How many minutes does the whole concert last, from the start of the first act to the end of the last act?
4.hint: Count the breaks carefully. There is one fewer break than there are acts.
4.why: 3 acts last 3 × 35 = 105 minutes. There are 2 breaks: 2 × 10 = 20 minutes. 105 + 20 = 125 minutes.

4.q: At a parade, the dancers wear badges in a row that keeps repeating this order: sun, moon, moon, star, star, cloud. Which badge does dancer number 83 wear?
4.hint: The pattern has 6 badges. How many full patterns fit before dancer number 83?
4.why: 83 = 13 full patterns of 6 badges and 5 more, because 13 × 6 = 78. The 5th badge of the pattern is star.

4.q: 8 rulers cost $18.40. A shop sells every ruler at the same price. How much do 5 rulers cost?
4.hint: Find the cost of 1 ruler first.
4.why: 1 ruler costs $2.30. 5 rulers cost 5 × $2.30 = $11.50.

4.q: The 3-digit number 5_4 has one hidden digit, and 3 divides the number exactly. Find the sum of all the digits that could fill the blank.
4.hint: A number divides by 3 exactly when its digits add up to a multiple of 3. Try each digit from 0 to 9.
4.why: 5 + 4 = 9. The blank digit must make 9 + digit a multiple of 3, so it is 0, 3, 6 or 9. The digits are 0, 3, 6, 9, and 0 + 3 + 6 + 9 = 18.

4.q: A rectangular noticeboard has a border of 108 cm all the way round its edge. The board is 31 cm long. How wide is the board?
4.hint: The two long sides use 31 + 31. What is left for the two short sides?

4.q: There are 30 coins that look the same. One of them is a fake and is a little heavier than the others. You have a balance scale that shows which side is heavier, or that both sides are equal. What is the fewest number of weighings that is certain to find the fake coin?
4.hint: Put the same number of coins on each side. What does the scale tell you if it balances, and what if it tips?
4.why: Each weighing splits the coins into three groups: the left pan, the right pan and the coins left out. The scale shows which group has the fake coin. Three weighings can handle 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 coins, which is not enough for 30. Four weighings can handle 81 coins, so 4 weighings are certain to work.

4.q: A school needs 2350 name tags. They are sold in packs of 8. How many packs must the school buy to have enough tags?
4.hint: Divide 2350 by 8. If there is a remainder, what must the school do?
4.why: 293 × 8 = 2344, so 6 name tags are still needed. 293 packs are not enough, so the school buys 294 packs.

4.q: The Rail Corridor trail is 4 km 85 m long. Give the length of the trail in metres.
4.hint: One kilometre is 1000 metres. Change the kilometres first.

4.q: Two shops sold 1250 mooncakes in all. Shop A sold 340 more mooncakes than Shop B. How many mooncakes did Shop A sell?
4.hint: Take away the extra 340. Share what is left equally between the two shops.
4.why: 1250 − 340 = 910. 910 ÷ 2 = 455 for Shop B. Shop A sold 455 + 340 = 795 mooncakes.

4.q: Two flags stand along a trail at 250 m and 874 m from the start. A water stop is exactly halfway between them. How far from the start is the water stop?
4.hint: Find how far apart the flags are. Half of that is the distance from each flag to the water stop.
4.why: The flags are 874 − 250 = 624 m apart. Half of 624 is 312. The water stop is 250 + 312 = 562 m.

4.q: Aunty needs 12 paintbrushes for her art class. Shop A sells packs of 3 paintbrushes for $10 a pack. Shop B sells paintbrushes at $6 each, but gives 1 paintbrush free for every 2 paintbrushes that you buy. Aunty chooses the cheaper shop. How much does she pay?
4.hint: Work out the cost at Shop A first. At Shop B, find how many paintbrushes of every 3 you pay for.
4.why: Shop A: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 packs, and 4 × $10 = $40. Shop B: every 3 paintbrushes cost 2 × $6 = $12, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 sets, so 4 × $12 = $48. The cheaper shop costs $40.

4.q: Mia writes the names of the numbers from one to twenty on cards. She puts the cards in alphabetical order, from A to Z. Which number is on card number 9 in her row?
4.hint: Write all twenty names. Sort them by their first letter, and look at the second letter when two names start the same.
4.why: In alphabetical order the names are eight, eighteen, eleven, fifteen, five, four, fourteen, nine, nineteen, one, seven, seventeen, six, sixteen, ten, thirteen, three, twelve, twenty, two. The 9th name is nineteen, which is the number 19.

4.q: Six children stand in a line. Their heights in centimetres, from the front to the back, are 140, 128, 145, 120, 125 and 135. The teacher wants them in order of height, from the shortest at the front to the tallest at the back. Only two children standing next to each other may swap places at one time. What is the fewest number of swaps?
4.hint: Look for pairs of children where a taller child stands in front of a shorter child. One swap of neighbours can fix only one such pair.
4.why: Count, for each child, the shorter children behind: 140 has 4, 128 has 2, 145 has 3, 120 has 0, 125 has 0, 135 has 0. 4 + 2 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 9. Each swap fixes one pair, so 9 swaps are needed.

4.q: A game stall has prizes that cost 1 point, 2 points, 3 points and so on, up to 40 points. Kai has only 3-point tokens and 7-point tokens, and the stall gives no change. How many of the 40 prizes can he pay for exactly?
4.hint: Find the prizes he cannot pay for. Try the small prices first, and then look for the price from which every price can be paid.
4.why: The prices he cannot pay are 1, 2, 4, 5, 8 and 11. From 12 upwards every price can be paid, for example 12 = 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, 13 = 3 + 3 + 7 and 14 = 7 + 7. That is 40 − 6 = 34 prizes.

4.q: Together, three classes collect 420 cans for recycling. Class B collects 60 more cans than Class A. Class C collects 90 more cans than Class A. How many cans does Class A collect?
4.hint: Take away the extra cans first. What is left is three equal shares.
4.why: The extras are 60 + 90 = 150 cans. Without them the total is 420 − 150 = 270, shared by 3 equal classes: 270 ÷ 3 = 90 cans.

4.q: A museum's gate counter recorded 1,246 visitors on Monday, 1,601 on Tuesday, 1,384 on Wednesday and 1,621 on Thursday. What was the total for the four days?
4.hint: Add the thousands, then the hundreds, then the tens and ones. Or add two days at a time.

4.q: Aisha, Ben, Chen and Dina each have a different hobby: painting, chess, swimming or violin. Aisha does not paint or play chess. Ben swims. Chen does not play the violin. Dina does not swim or paint. Who plays chess?
4.hint: Ben swims, so nobody else does. Then see what is left for each person.
4.why: Aisha has the hobby of violin, Ben has the hobby of swimming, Chen has the hobby of painting, Dina has the hobby of chess. So Dina plays chess.

4.q: In the diagram, some squares are shaded. The thick line is a line of symmetry, so the left side and the right side must match like twins in a mirror. How many extra squares have to be shaded to make the diagram symmetrical?
4.hint: Take each shaded square in turn. Where is its mirror partner on the other side of the thick line?
4.why: Each shaded square needs a shaded partner on the other side of the line. The first row needs 1 more, the second row 2, the third row 0 and the fourth row 2. That is 5 squares.

4.q: At an ice-cream stall, a sundae has one flavour, one sauce and one topping. The stall offers 3 flavours, 4 sauces and 5 toppings. How many different sundaes can be made?
4.hint: Choose a flavour and a sauce first. How many pairs is that? Then add the topping.
4.why: 3 flavours × 4 sauces = 12 pairs. Each pair can have 5 toppings: 12 × 5 = 60 sundaes.

4.q: Priya is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Mei Ling. Mei Ling is taller than Ravi. Ravi is taller than Sam. Who is in the middle?
4.hint: Write the five names in a row from shortest to tallest.
4.why: From shortest to tallest: Sam, Ravi, Mei Ling, Ben, Priya. The one in the middle is Mei Ling.

4.q: A quilt is sewn from patches in 14 rows of 15 patches. Red and white patches alternate along every row and every column, and the patch in the top left corner is red. How many white patches are in the quilt?
4.hint: Count all the patches first. Red and white patches alternate.
4.why: There are 14 × 15 = 210 patches. Red and white alternate and 210 is an even number, so exactly half are white: 210 ÷ 2 = 105 patches.

4.q: Dina has a three-digit number. Its hundreds digit is 2 and its tens digit is 5. When she swaps the hundreds digit and the ones digit, the number becomes 396 bigger. What was her number?
4.hint: Swapping the hundreds digit and the ones digit changes the number by the same amount as the difference of the two digits times 99.
4.why: 396 ÷ 99 = 4, so the ones digit is 4 more than the hundreds digit: 2 + 4 = 6. The number is 256. Check: 652 − 256 = 396.

4.q: At a community fair, 14 stallholders greet each other. Every two stallholders bow to each other exactly once. How many bows are there in all?
4.hint: Each stallholder bows to all the others, but a bow between two stallholders is counted once only.
4.why: The first stallholder makes 13 bows, the next makes 12 new ones, then 11, and so on down to 1. 13 + 12 + 11 + ... + 1 = 91 bows.

4.q: Mia and Ben play a number game. They take turns to say a number from 1 to 6, and each new number is added to the running total. Mia says the first number. Whoever makes the total exactly 53 wins. What number should Mia say first to be sure of winning?
4.hint: Think backwards from 53. Which totals can you make so that your friend cannot stop you reaching 53?
4.why: Mia says 4, which leaves 49 to go, a multiple of 7. Whatever number Ben says, Mia says a number that makes 7 in that round. After the last round the total is exactly 53 and Mia wins.

4.q: Farhan has $94 and Hui Min has $52. Farhan gives Hui Min some money, and then they have the same amount. How many dollars does Farhan give?
4.hint: Find how many more dollars Farhan has. Each dollar he gives moves across the gap.
4.why: Farhan has $42 more. Each dollar given makes the gap 2 smaller, so he gives half of 42, which is 21 dollars. Check: they both have $73.

4.q: Hui Min has 72 stamps. 5/8 of her stamps are from Singapore. How many of her stamps are from Singapore?
4.hint: Find 1/8 of the stamps first. Then think about how many eighths you need.
4.why: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, so 1/8 of the stamps is 9. 5 eighths is 5 × 9 = 45 stamps.

5.q: On Saturday, Daniel cycles 12.75 km. On Sunday he cycles 8.9 km. How far does he cycle altogether?
5.hint: Write 8.9 as 8.90, and line up the decimal points.

5.q: A 3-digit number is a climbing number if each digit is bigger than the digit before it, like 358. How many 3-digit climbing numbers are there?
5.hint: No climbing number can have a 0, because a 0 in the tens or ones place would be smaller than the digit before. Choose 3 different digits from 1 to 9 and write them in order.
5.why: Each set of 3 different digits from 1 to 9 gives exactly one climbing number. There are 9 × 8 × 7 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 504 ÷ 6 = 84 numbers.

5.q: A ship sails 14 km north, then 13 km west, then 6 km south. The sea lanes run only north-south or east-west. What is the fewest number of kilometres the ship must sail along the lanes to get back to its port?
5.hint: Find how far north or south of the port the ship is now, and how far east or west.
5.why: North 14 and south 6 leave the ship 14 − 6 = 8 km north of the port. It is also 13 km west. To get back it must sail 8 km south and 13 km east: 8 + 13 = 21 km.

5.q: Four runners take turns in a relay race. Their legs take 1 minute 52 seconds, 2 minutes 8 seconds, 1 minute 47 seconds and 2 minutes 3 seconds. How many seconds does the whole relay take?
5.hint: Change each leg to seconds first. One minute is 60 seconds.
5.why: 1 min 52 s is 112 s, 2 min 8 s is 128 s, 1 min 47 s is 107 s and 2 min 3 s is 123 s. 112 + 128 + 107 + 123 = 470 seconds.

5.q: A number is divided by 13. The quotient is 27 and the remainder is 9. Add 50 to the number and divide the new number by 13. What is the new quotient?
5.hint: First find the number. It is made of full groups of 13 and the remainder.
5.why: 27 × 13 = 351, and 351 + 9 = 360. Adding 50 gives 410. 410 ÷ 13 is 31 with a remainder, so the new quotient is 31.

5.q: Ali, Ben, Chen, Dina and Emily each choose a different club: robotics, art, choir, chess or drama. Ali chooses neither art nor drama. Ben chooses chess. Chen chooses neither robotics nor drama. Dina chooses none of art, choir or robotics. Emily chooses neither art nor choir. Who chooses robotics?
5.hint: Ben has chess, so nobody else does. Then work through what each remaining person can choose.
5.why: Ali chooses choir, Ben chooses chess, Chen chooses art, Dina chooses drama, Emily chooses robotics. So Emily chooses robotics.

5.q: Dad's old watch runs fast: in 60 minutes of real time it shows 70 minutes. He sets it right at noon. Later the watch shows that 280 minutes have gone by. How many minutes of real time have gone by?
5.hint: In 60 real minutes the watch shows 70 minutes. How many sets of 70 minutes are in 280 minutes?
5.why: 280 ÷ 70 = 4, so 4 real hours have gone by. 4 × 60 = 240 minutes.

5.q: A flight leaves at 23:35 and lands at 03:10 the next day. How many minutes is the flight?
5.hint: Count the time from 23:35 to midnight. Then add the time from midnight to 03:10.
5.why: From 23:35 to midnight is 25 minutes. From midnight to 03:10 is 190 minutes. 25 + 190 = 215 minutes.

5.q: Mei adds 7 odd numbers and 4 even numbers, all different. Is her answer odd or even?
5.hint: Try small numbers first, such as 3 + 5 + 7 + 2 + 4. Pair up the numbers that are not even and see what each pair makes.
5.why: The 7 odd numbers make 3 pairs and 1 odd number left. Each pair adds to an even number, so the odd numbers together make an odd number. Even numbers never change whether a number is odd or even. The answer is odd.

5.q: A shop's price board lights up each digit with bars, as the table shows. The board shows every price from $100 to $109, one after another. How many bars does it light up altogether? (Count only the digits, not the dollar sign.)
5.hint: Count the bars in the hundreds digit, the tens digit and the ones digits separately, then add.
5.why: The hundreds digit is 1 in all 10 prices: 10 × 2 = 20 bars. The tens digit is 0 in all 10 prices: 10 × 6 = 60 bars. The ones digits are 0 to 9, which use 6 + 2 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 7 + 6 = 49 bars. 20 + 60 + 49 = 129 bars.

5.q: At a beach shop, a pail, a spade and a ball each have a fixed price in whole dollars. A pail and a spade cost $14 together. A spade and 2 balls cost $12 together. 2 pails and a ball cost $19 together. What does a spade cost?
5.hint: Try a price for the ball. Then use the second line to find the spade, and check the other two lines.
5.why: If a ball costs $3, the second line gives a spade of 12 − 6 = $6. The first line then gives a pail of 14 − 6 = $8. The third line checks: 2 × 8 + 3 = 19. A spade costs $6.

5.q: A table shows how many visitors came through six zoo gates one Sunday: Gate 1 412, Gate 2 358, Gate 3 507, Gate 4 296, Gate 5 444 and Gate 6 381. How many more visitors came through the busiest gate than through the quietest gate?
5.hint: Find the biggest number and the smallest number first.
5.why: The busiest gate had 507 visitors and the quietest gate had 296 visitors. 507 − 296 = 211 visitors.

5.q: 10 children stand in a circle and are numbered 1 to 10 going clockwise. Counting starts at child 1. Every 3rd child sits down, and the counting carries on round the circle, skipping the children who are already sitting. Which numbered child is the last one standing?
5.hint: Write down the children in a row. Cross off every third child, carry on from where you stopped, and keep going round.
5.why: The children sit down in this order: 3, 6, 9, 2, 7, 1, 8, 5, 10. The last child standing is number 4.

5.q: Two buoys float in a channel, 1,240 m and 2,036 m from the pier. A rescue boat is anchored at the exact middle point between the two buoys. How many metres is the boat from the pier?
5.hint: Find how far apart the buoys are. Half of that is the distance from each buoy to the boat.
5.why: The buoys are 2036 − 1240 = 796 m apart. Half of 796 is 398. The boat is 1240 + 398 = 1638 m from the pier.

5.q: 7 friends sit round a circular table. Turning everyone round the table by the same number of seats does not make a new seating plan. How many different seating plans are there?
5.hint: Fix one friend in one seat. Then the other friends can be arranged in the seats that remain.
5.why: Fix one friend. The other 6 friends can fill the other seats in 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 ways, which is 720 plans.

5.q: A town has 12 bus stops. Every pair of stops is joined by its own direct bus route. How many bus routes are there?
5.hint: Each stop has a route to 12 − 1 other stops, but every route joins two stops.
5.why: Each of the 12 stops has a route to 11 other stops, which makes 132. Every route was counted twice, so 132 ÷ 2 = 66 routes.

5.q: A box of red pens has 4 times as many pens as a box of blue pens. Together the two boxes hold 85 pens. How many pens are in the box of red pens?
5.hint: Draw one bar for the blue pens and a bar 4 times as long for the red pens.
5.why: Blue is 1 part and red is 4 parts, so there are 5 parts. 85 ÷ 5 = 17 blue pens. Red: 4 × 17 = 68 pens.

5.q: A hiker starts at a camp that is 450 m above sea level. All her changes in height are in metres. She climbs up by 120, then goes down by 85, then climbs up by 240, then goes down by 60. How high above sea level is she at the end, in metres?
5.hint: Write down the height above sea level after each change.
5.why: The heights in order are 450, 570, 485, 725, 665. At the end she is 665 m above sea level.

5.q: A fruit seller sold half of her mangoes in the morning. In the afternoon she sold 12 more. She has 19 mangoes left. How many mangoes did she have at the start of the day?
5.hint: Work backwards. Put back the mangoes sold in the afternoon. Then double.
5.why: Put back the 12: 19 + 12 = 31. These are half of the mangoes, so double: 31 × 2 = 62 mangoes.

5.q: Trails in kilometres join six places in a park: Camp to Lake 12. Camp to Ridge 10. Lake to Ridge 4. Lake to Cave 16. Ridge to Cave 20. Ridge to Peak 26. Cave to Peak 6. What is the shortest way from Camp to Peak, in kilometres?
5.hint: List the routes from Camp to Peak, and add up the trail lengths on each route.
5.why: The best route is Camp-Lake-Cave-Peak: 12 + 16 + 6 = 34 km. Camp-Ridge-Peak is 10 + 26 = 36, and Camp-Ridge-Cave-Peak is 10 + 20 + 6 = 36.

5.q: 26 scouts must cross a river in a boat that holds at most 5 people. The boat cannot cross by itself, so at least one scout must row it each time. How many crossings does the boat make in all, counting the trips back as well as the trips across?
5.hint: The boat can carry 5 scouts, but one scout must row back after every crossing except the last. How many scouts can one trip across and one trip back move for good?
5.why: Each trip across and back moves 5 − 1 = 4 scouts across for good, because one scout rows back. The last crossing carries 5 scouts and needs no trip back. So 26 − 5 = 21 scouts must be moved by round trips, and 21 ÷ 4 is more than 5, so 6 round trips are needed. 6 round trips are 6 × 2 = 12 crossings, and the last crossing makes it 13 crossings.

5.q: A culture of bacteria has 250 cells. The number of cells doubles every hour. How many cells are there after 6 hours?
5.hint: Double the number for each hour. Or multiply by 2 as many times as there are hours.
5.why: The number doubles 6 times: 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000. After 6 hours there are 16,000 cells.

5.q: Zara adds up the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, all the way to 100. Her answer is 5036, but she skipped one number by mistake. Which number did she skip?
5.hint: Find the correct total first. Pair 1 with the biggest number, 2 with the next biggest, and so on.
5.why: There are 100 ÷ 2 = 50 pairs, and each pair adds up to 1 + 100 = 101. The correct total is 50 × 101 = 5050. 5050 − 5036 = 14.

5.q: Mei Ling has 215 stamps and Ben has 143 stamps. Mei Ling hands some stamps to Ben so that each child ends up with the same number. How many stamps does she hand over?
5.hint: Find how many more stamps Mei Ling has. Each stamp she gives moves across the gap.
5.why: Mei Ling has 72 more. Each stamp given makes the gap 2 smaller, so she gives half of 72, which is 36 stamps. Check: they both have 179.

5.q: A garden bed has four straight sides. Three of its corner angles are 95°, 110° and 70°. The four corner angles of a bed like this add up to 360°. How big is the fourth corner angle?
5.hint: Add the three angles you know. Then take the total away from 360°.

5.q: A line graph joins the measured heights of a young tree each December: 120 cm, 135 cm, 158 cm, 170 cm and 205 cm. In its best year, by how many centimetres did the tree gain?
5.hint: Take each December reading away from the next one to find the gain in each year.
5.why: The gains are 15, 23, 12, 35. The best year gave 35 cm.

5.q: A club of 9 members chooses a president, a secretary and a treasurer. No member can have two jobs. In how many different ways can the three jobs be filled?
5.hint: Choose the president first. Then see how many members are left for secretary.
5.why: 9 choices for president, 8 for secretary and 7 for treasurer. 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 ways.

5.q: Each bag of flour weighs 0.35 kg. Aunty buys 12 bags. Find the total weight of the flour in kilograms.
5.hint: Multiply 35 × 12 first. Then think about where the decimal point goes.

5.q: The page numbers of six pages that follow each other add up to 255. What is the smallest page number?
5.hint: Call the smallest page number n. The others are n + 1, n + 2, up to n + 5.
5.why: The six numbers add to 6n + 15 = 255. So 6n = 240 and n = 40.

5.q: A frog sits on the top-left lily pad of a pond. It hops only to the pad on its right or the pad below it, and it makes 4 hops right and 3 hops down in all, in any order, to reach the bottom-right pad. A boat covers the pad that is 2 pads right and 1 pad down from the start, so the frog cannot land there. How many different ways can the frog reach the bottom-right pad?
5.hint: First count all the ways when no pad is covered. Then take away the ways that land on the covered pad.
5.why: All ways: 35. Ways through the covered pad: 3 ways to reach it × 6 ways to go on from it = 18. 35 − 18 = 17 ways.

5.q: A printer sets the numbers 1 to 480 in type, one number for each page of a catalogue. One digit is one piece of type. How many pieces of type does the printer need?
5.hint: Group the numbers by how many digits they have: one digit, two digits, three digits.
5.why: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 pieces. Pages 10 to 99 are 90 pages with 2 pieces each, which is 180. Pages 100 to 480 are 381 pages with 3 pieces each, which is 1143. 9 + 180 + 1143 = 1332 pieces.

6.q: Kumar and Aisha begin at the two ends of a 2,400 m path and walk towards each other at the same time. Kumar covers 70 m per minute and Aisha covers 90 m per minute. When do they meet? Answer in minutes.
6.hint: Each minute, the gap between them shrinks by both of their distances added together.
6.why: Each minute the gap shrinks by 160 m. 2,400 ÷ 160 = 15 minutes.

6.q: Ali, Ben, Chen, Dina, Emily and Farid each play a different sport: hockey, netball, tennis, cricket, rugby or golf. Ali plays rugby. Ben plays neither hockey nor netball. Chen plays golf. Dina does not play hockey or tennis. Emily plays neither netball nor cricket. Farid plays neither hockey nor netball. Ben does not play cricket. Who plays cricket?
6.hint: Start with the people whose sports are known. Then cross out those sports for everyone else.
6.why: Ali plays rugby, Ben plays tennis, Chen plays golf, Dina plays netball, Emily plays hockey, Farid plays cricket. So Farid plays cricket.

6.q: A banner is a triangle with an area of 132 square centimetres. One side, the base, is 24 cm long. How tall is the banner, measured straight up from that base?
6.hint: Area of a triangle is half of base times height. So base times height is twice the area.
6.why: Twice the area is 2 × 132 = 264. Base times height = 264, so the height is 264 ÷ 24 = 11 cm.

6.q: Look at the number 83,246. Mei swaps its first digit and its last digit. By how much does the number change?
6.hint: Write the new number. Then find the difference between the two numbers.
6.why: Swapping the first and last digits of 83,246 gives 63,248. 83,246 − 63,248 = 19,998.

6.q: A jeweller has a tray of pearls that all look the same. One pearl is hollow, so it is lighter than the others. She has a two-pan scale. What is the greatest number of pearls in the tray for which she is certain to find the hollow pearl using only 6 weighings?
6.hint: Each weighing can sort the pearls into three equal groups. How many groups can you tell apart after one weighing, two weighings, and so on?
6.why: One weighing tells you which of 3 groups holds the hollow pearl. Each extra weighing multiplies the number of pearls by 3. After 6 weighings the greatest number is 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 729 pearls.

6.q: Mei cycles at 15 km/h for 2 hours 20 minutes. How far does she cycle?
6.hint: Change 2 hours 20 minutes into hours. 20 minutes is 1/3 of an hour.
6.why: 2 hours 20 minutes is 2 1/3 hours. Distance = speed × time = 15 × 2 1/3 = 35 km.

6.q: Aisha starts a money jar with $5 on day 1. Each day the amount in the jar is doubled. How many dollars are in the jar on day 9?
6.hint: Write the amount for each day. Double the last amount each time.
6.why: Doubling 8 times starting from 5: 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1280. On day 9 the jar has $1280.

6.q: Six library books stand side by side on a shelf. The numbers of pages in the books, from left to right, are 220, 80, 140, 170, 100 and 240. The librarian wants the books from the fewest pages to the most pages. She can exchange only two books that stand next to each other at one time. What is the smallest number of exchanges?
6.hint: Count the pairs of books where the book on the left has more pages than the book on the right. One exchange of neighbours can fix only one such pair.
6.why: Count, for each book, the books to its right with fewer pages: 220 has 4, 80 has 0, 140 has 1, 170 has 1, 100 has 0, 240 has 0. 4 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 6. Each exchange fixes one pair, so 6 exchanges are needed.

6.q: The 4-digit number 4_7_ has the same digit hidden in both blanks. It divides exactly by 6. Add together every digit that could be hidden.
6.hint: A number divides by 6 exactly when it is even and its digits add up to a multiple of 3. Try each digit from 0 to 9.
6.why: The number is even, so the hidden digit is even. The digits of 4_7_ add up to 4 + 7 + 2 × (hidden digit) = 11 + 2 × (hidden digit), which must be a multiple of 3. The digits that work are 2, 8. 2 + 8 = 10.

6.q: In this pattern, every number after the first two equals the previous two added together: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ... Which number is the 12th one?
6.hint: Add the last two numbers to get the next one. Keep going.

6.q: A pipe is 7/8 m long. It is sawn into short pieces that are each 1/32 m long. How many short pieces are there?
6.hint: Dividing by 1/32 is the same as multiplying by 32. Or ask how many 32nds are in 7/8.

6.q: Hui Min and Kumar share $480 in the ratio 5 : 3. How much money does the one with the bigger share get?
6.hint: Add the parts of the ratio to see how many equal parts there are.
6.why: 5 + 3 = 8 parts. 1 part is $480 ÷ 8 = $60. The bigger share is 5 parts: 5 × $60 = $300.

6.q: Tin A holds 4 times as much paint as Tin B. Tin A holds 45 mL more paint than Tin B. How many millilitres of paint does Tin A hold?
6.hint: Draw one bar for Tin B and a bar 4 times as long for Tin A. How many parts is the difference?
6.why: Tin B is 1 part and Tin A is 4 parts. The difference is 3 parts and it is 45 mL. 1 part = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 mL. Tin A holds 4 × 15 = 60 mL.

6.q: A national park counted 1,386,725 visitors in one year. A newspaper reports the figure to the nearest ten thousand. What figure does the newspaper report?
6.hint: Look at the thousands digit. Is it 5 or more?
6.why: The thousands digit is 6, so the ten thousands go up by one: 1,386,725 rounds to 1,390,000.

6.q: A librarian packs books into crates of 19. She fills 24 full crates and has 7 books left over. Then 150 more books arrive. She puts all the books together and packs them again in crates of 19. How many full crates does she have now?
6.hint: First find how many books the librarian had at the start. Then add the new books.
6.why: 24 × 19 = 456, and 456 + 7 = 463 books at the start. With 150 more, she has 613 books. 613 ÷ 19 is 32 with a remainder, so she can fill 32 crates.

6.q: In three quizzes, Siti scored 78, 84 and 90. What score does she need in the fourth quiz to have a mean score of exactly 85?
6.hint: A mean of 85 over 4 quizzes means the four scores add up to a certain total.
6.why: The four scores must add up to 340. Her first three add up to 252. 340 − 252 = 88 marks.

6.q: Dan fills a water tank 5/6 full. He uses 2/5 of the water in the tank to wash the car. What fraction of a full tank does he use?
6.hint: Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms, then simplify.
6.why: 2/5 × 5/6 = 10/30, and 10/30 is the same as 1/3. He uses 1/3 of a full tank.

6.q: A teacher picks 3 pupils from a group of 8 to make a quiz team. The order does not matter. How many different teams can she pick?
6.hint: If the order mattered there would be 8 × 7 × 6 choices. How many orders does each team of 3 have?
6.why: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ordered choices. Each team of 3 is counted 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times, so the number of teams is 336 ÷ 6 = 56 teams.

6.q: A line graph shows the money in Ravi's savings box at the end of each month: $11, $16, $45, $42, $50 and $48. What was the biggest rise from one month to the next?
6.hint: Find the change between each pair of neighbouring months. Look only at the rises.
6.why: From month to month the money changed by +5, +29, −3, +8, −2 dollars (a plus sign is a rise and a minus sign is a fall). The biggest rise is $29.

6.q: Emily is taller than Dina. Farid is taller than Emily. Dina is taller than Chen. Chen is taller than Ali. Who is taller than Dina but shorter than Farid?
6.hint: Write the five names in a row from tallest to shortest.
6.why: From tallest to shortest: Farid, Emily, Dina, Chen, Ali. Emily is between Farid and Dina.

6.q: a, b and c stand for whole numbers. a + b = 47, b + c = 58 and a + c = 55. What number does a stand for?
6.hint: Add the three sums together. Every letter then appears twice. What do you get for a + b + c?
6.why: Adding the three sums: 2 × (a + b + c) = 47 + 58 + 55 = 160, so a + b + c = 80. Then a = 80 − 58 = 22.

6.q: The ratio of Ali's stickers to Ben's stickers is 2 : 3. Ali buys 10 more stickers. Then the ratio of Ali's stickers to Ben's stickers is 3 : 4. How many stickers does Ben have?
6.hint: Ben's stickers do not change. Let one unit of the first ratio be u stickers, and write Ali's new number in terms of u.
6.why: Let one unit be u stickers. Ali has 2u and Ben has 3u. After Ali buys 10 more, Ali has 2u + 10. The new ratio is 3 : 4, so 4 × (2u + 10) = 3 × 3u, which is 8u + 40 = 9u. So u = 40. Ben has 3 × 40 = 120 stickers.

6.q: The mean mark of 20 pupils in Class A is 70. The mean mark of 30 pupils in Class B is 80. What is the mean mark of all 50 pupils together?
6.hint: Do not just average the two means, because Class B has more pupils. Find the total marks of each class first.
6.why: Class A: 20 × 70 = 1400 marks. Class B: 30 × 80 = 2400 marks. Together: 1400 + 2400 = 3800 marks for 50 pupils. 3800 ÷ 50 = 76 marks.

6.q: A school council has 11 students. A head, a deputy and a helper are chosen from the students, and nobody can do two jobs. In how many different ways can the three places be filled?
6.hint: Choose the head first. Then see how many students are left for deputy.
6.why: 11 choices for head, then 10 for deputy, then 9 for helper. 11 × 10 × 9 = 990 ways.

6.q: A regular decagon has 10 equal sides and 10 equal angles. How big is each angle inside the decagon?
6.hint: A polygon with n sides can be split into n − 2 triangles. Each triangle has angles that add to 180°.
6.why: A decagon splits into 8 triangles: 8 × 180° = 1440°. Share among 10 equal angles: 1440° ÷ 10 = 144°.

6.q: Aisha scored 54 out of 72 marks in a test. What percentage did she score?
6.hint: Write the score as a fraction of the whole. Then change it to a percentage.

6.q: Jun's coach pays him $4 for the first game he plays this season, $8 for the second game, $12 for the third game, and every game after that pays $4 more than the game before. The last game pays $120. How many dollars does Jun earn altogether?
6.hint: Pair the first game with the last game, the second game with the one before the last, and so on.
6.why: There are 30 games. Each pair adds to $4 + $120 = $124. 15 pairs make 15 × $124 = $1860.

6.q: At 5:40 pm a ferry sails from the terminal to an island, and the crossing takes 5 hours 35 minutes. Timetables show times in 24-hour time. Write the arrival time as four digits, like 0915.
6.hint: Change the start time to 24-hour time first: add 12 to the hour for a pm time.
6.why: 5:40 pm is 1740 in 24-hour time. Five hours later is 2240. Then 35 more minutes make 2315. The timetable shows 2315.

6.q: Count the pairs of prime numbers that add up to 124. For example, 11 + 113 is one pair, and 113 + 11 is not counted again.
6.hint: List the primes below 60. For each one, check whether 124 minus that prime is also a prime.

6.q: How many factors does 360 have? Count 1 and 360 as factors.
6.hint: Write 360 as a product of prime numbers first. Then use the powers to count the factors.
6.why: 360 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5, so 2 appears 3 times, 3 appears 2 times and 5 appears once. The number of factors is (3 + 1) × (2 + 1) × (1 + 1) = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 factors.

6.q: What is the sum of all the whole numbers from −8 to 11, including −8 and 11?
6.hint: Look for numbers that cancel each other out.
6.why: The numbers from −8 to 8 cancel in pairs, giving 0. That leaves 9 + 10 + 11 = 30.
